newsitem.title: USA: IPAI urged to report separate China aluminum data.
newsitem.headline: IPAI urged to report separate China aluminum data.

text.p: Insistence by International Primary Aluminium Institute that Chinese aluminum production data should not be reported separately from the rest of Asia is unsettling the light metal market, analyst Jim Southwood of Commodity Metals Management said.
"We believe that China should not be included in the 'Asian' area of IPAI data," Southwood said. "By doing so, the IPAI is contributing to the uncertainty and volatility of the market."
From January the IPAI included China and Tajikistan, "without warning," to the Asian region figure for monthly primary aluminum production.
But no figures were given for December to give an indication of change in output, Southwood said in his March issue of Aluminum Overview.
Southwood said data from China varied tremedously and upset the ability to spot accurate trends.
He said latest figures from Chinese state agencies showed that February production was at an annual rate of 1.976 million tonnes compared to 1.7 million tonnes in January.
"That's a 300,000 tonne shift month to month, which is impossible," Southwood said.
By looking at global, historical data, CMM estimated that global smelting output only grew about 50,000 tonnes in January, not the two million tonnes reported by IPAI.
Southwood said the IPAI's argument that China should not be reported separately because a single producer may be recognised, was not valid.
"With numerous producers in China, no single producer could be identified, therefore this 'policy' does not apply," Southwood said.
Asia was adding aluminum capacity faster than any other region and it was important to separate out China. The IPAI was obscuring the view of new capacity additions.

"Because Chinese production is normally not exported, Western producers and consumers should be interested in how much is produced in the rest of Asia where metal is normally exported into the free market," Southwood added.

CMM said IPAI's January data was "questionable", because output in Oceania fell despite a smelter expansion at Tiwai Point, while output in Africa, North America, Western Europe and Latin America were unchanged.
CMM said an increase of 400,000 tonnes or so is the most that can be expected from new capacity in 1997. This represents a 2.5 percent increase in Western world smelter output.
Southwood urged aluminum industry officials to lobby the IPAI to changes its policy on reporting China data.
